The Raising of Lazarus
thuh RAY-zing uhv LAZ-uh-ruhs
noun (miracle of Christ)
From the Greek Lazaros, from the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped"; the raising of Lazarus of Bethany from the dead by Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

The raising of Lazarus is the great sign recorded in John 11, wherein the Lord Jesus called His friend Lazarus, four days dead and already in the tomb, back to life by the word of His power. To the grieving Martha He declared, "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Coming to the grave, He "cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth" (John 11:43-44). This was no swoon nor mere recovery, but a true raising of one whose body had begun to corrupt, a manifest display of Christ's sovereign dominion over death itself. Yet the same sign that gave life to Lazarus hardened the Sanhedrin against the Lord, for from that day "they took counsel together for to put him to death" (John 11:53), and they plotted to slay Lazarus also (John 12:10). Thus the giving of life provoked the counsel of murder, and the road to the cross was set. This dictionary confesses that in the raising of Lazarus we behold a pledge of the general resurrection and a proof that He who is the Resurrection and the Life will surely call all His own from their graves at the last day.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The raising of Lazarus is Christ's calling of his friend, four days dead, from the tomb in John 11. It displayed His power over death and His claim, "I am the resurrection, and the life." The sign hardened the Sanhedrin to seek His death.

expand to see more

THE RAISING OF LAZARUS, noun. The miracle by which Christ called Lazarus of Bethany, four days dead, alive from the grave.

It was wrought by His mere word, "Lazarus, come forth," in the presence of many witnesses at Bethany.

"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25).

It manifests His sovereign power over death and is a pledge of the resurrection of His people.

Its consequence: the chief priests, enraged rather than believing, took counsel to put Him to death.

📖 Key Scripture

John 11:25 — "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:"

John 11:43 — "And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth."

John 11:44 — "And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."

John 11:53 — "Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition; the critical academy denies the miracle as legend, while the church receives it as sober history and a pledge of the resurrection to come.

expand to see more

The critical mind, ruling out the supernatural beforehand, treats the raising of Lazarus as a Johannine invention, a theological symbol rather than a historical event, since it cannot allow that a man four days dead was truly called from the tomb. But John writes as an eyewitness of glory, recording the place, the names, the weeping, and the stench of death, and the response of the rulers who could not deny the sign and so resolved to kill both the Lord and Lazarus. To deny the event is to call the apostle a liar.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over death and the certainty of the resurrection. Lazarus came forth still bound in graveclothes, raised to die again; but he is a pledge of that greater raising, when the dead in Christ shall rise incorruptible. He who said "I am the resurrection, and the life" will speak the same word over every grave that holds His own, and they shall hear His voice and live.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek Lazaros, a form of the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped"; the account is given wholly in John 11 and 12.

expand to see more

Lazarus is the Greek Lazaros, contracted from the Hebrew Eleazar, "God hath helped."

He was of Bethany, brother to Martha and Mary, and is called the friend whom Jesus loved (John 11:3).

The phrase "come forth" renders the Greek deuro exo, a direct command of the living voice of Christ.

"The resurrection" here is the Greek anastasis, the very life of which Christ is the source.

The four days in the tomb (John 11:39) underscore the reality and finality of the death undone.

Usage

"In the raising of Lazarus the Lord proved that He is the Resurrection and the Life."

"The raising of Lazarus, far from softening the rulers, hardened their resolve to kill the Lord."

"Lazarus came forth bound in graveclothes, a living pledge of the resurrection of all the saints."
